title: Communication habits that keep a build on track
metaTitle: Communication that keeps a build on track
excerpt: Keep a build on track with one shared channel, decisions written down, and a cadence both sides keep. Clear updates and honest timelines prevent late surprises.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table. The shared table is the point: one place where the work and the decisions sit together.
caption: One table, one thread, decisions you can find. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How many channels should a studio project use?
faqs.answer: Use one channel for day-to-day work, plus email when you need a record outside that tool. Decisions that change the date or the scope get written in the shared place, even if they started on a call. A second group chat for “quick questions” becomes the place where the real project hides.

faqs.question: What should a weekly update include?
faqs.answer: Include what moved, what is blocked, and whether the date still holds. Name the next decision you need and who owes it. If something slipped, say what slipped and what you recommend. A update that only says “going well” is not a cadence.

faqs.question: What does an honest timeline sound like?
faqs.answer: It names the date, the assumption, and the consequence of a late decision. Homepage copy by Thursday keeps the review on Monday, and copy on Monday moves that review. A date with no assumption is a wish.

markdown:
Working with a design studio stays on track when three habits are boring and consistent: one shared channel, a written decision for anything that changes the work, and a cadence both sides keep.

Hanabi’s standard is the practical version of that. Clear updates, honest timelines, and fewer surprises. The surprises that hurt are not the small visual tweaks. They are a date that moved in someone’s head, a scope that grew in a side thread, and a review that arrives after the work has already turned.

## One channel

Pick the place where the project lives. A single chat, a single project tool, or a single email thread with a clear subject. Everyone who can approve, and everyone who is making the work, can open it.

Side channels are how builds drift. A text message that changes the homepage, a comment in a design file nobody else sees, a call with no note. The work may still happen. The other people on the project will design and build the previous version. Then you will pay for the merge.

Calls are still useful. They are a bad archive. If a call changes a page, a date, or a priority, one person writes the decision in the channel the same day. Two or three sentences. What we decided. What we are not doing. Who owns the next step.

Keep the client and the studio in the same channel. A studio-only thread for logistics is fine. A studio-only thread for the actual design direction means the founder hears the conclusion after the hours are spent. Hanabi’s preference is plain communication in the open: the constraint, the recommendation, and the ask.

Files belong where the work is, not as attachments that fork. Design in a shared Figma. Code in the repository you will own. Brand files and notes in a place you can find after launch, such as a client portal. The channel links to those. It does not become a second copy of them.

## The written decision

A decision is a sentence someone can build from. “Make it more premium” is a mood. “Use the quieter type, drop the second illustration, and keep the offer in the first screen” is a decision.

Write decisions when they change one of four things: the words a stranger sees, the pages or flows in scope, the date, or the way the thing is built. Small polish inside an agreed direction can live in the file. The four items above should not live only in memory.

Give each decision an owner and a status. Proposed, accepted, or parked. Parked is a gift. It lets a good idea exist without entering this week’s build. Accepted means the studio can spend time on it and the founder will not be surprised by the result.

Disagreement belongs in the same note. If the studio thinks a requested page will hide the offer, say that next to the request, with the alternative. If the founder wants the page anyway, the written decision records the trade. Later reviews can point at the sentence. They do not have to relive the meeting.

Speed is one of the things worth writing down in shared language. Google’s [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) give you that language: largest contentful paint within 2.5 seconds, interaction to next paint within 200 milliseconds, and cumulative layout shift under 0.1. You do not need those numbers in every update. You do need them when someone asks for a heavier hero, a new animation, or a third-party widget. The decision can say “we will add it if the page still meets those targets on the template.” That keeps “it feels slow” from becoming a late surprise.

## A cadence

Cadence is a rhythm people can plan around. For most studio builds, a weekly working review plus a short written update is enough. Daily standups are rarely the missing piece. A missing decision is.

The weekly note can be short.

- What moved since the last note.
- What is waiting on the founder, by name.
- What is waiting on the studio.
- Whether the date holds, and the one risk if it might not.

The review looks at work against the brief, not at a tour of every frame. Bring the page, the sentence it is supposed to make true, and the open decision. End with the next date you will look again. A review that does not produce a next step will be repeated, louder, three days later.

Match the cadence to the phase. Early on, you may need two touches a week because the direction is still moving. During build, once a week is often right, with async notes in between for specific questions. Near launch, the cadence tightens around a checklist: staging, content freeze, DNS, the person watching the first hour. Say that shift before it happens so nobody thinks the project went quiet.

Silence is a signal. If the studio owes an update and the day passes, the founder should ask once, in the channel. If the founder owes copy or access and the day passes, the studio should say what moved on the date. Polite waiting is how a week disappears. Hanabi’s honest timeline includes that nudge. Fewer surprises means saying the slip while there is still a way to use the remaining time.

## What an honest timeline includes

A date without assumptions is a slogan. An honest timeline names both.

“We will review the homepage on the 12th if we have the offer sentence and the photos by the 8th.” That sentence tells the founder what their delay costs. It also tells the studio they may not invent the copy and call it approved.

Include dependencies you do not control: a payment-provider review, a legal read, a domain unlock. Put them on the timeline when you know about them, not when they block the launch on Friday. Access is the common one. A project that cannot enter the current site, the analytics, or the store admin will spend the first days waiting. Say that at kickoff, and repeat it if the access is still missing.

When the date must move, move it in writing, with the reason and the new date. Do not let it slide in a series of “almost.” Almost is how trust erodes. A new date is a fact both sides can hold.

Range estimates belong early. False precision belongs nowhere. Once the slice is known, the timeline can tighten. Until then, “this phase is two weeks, assuming feedback within two working days” is more professional than a calendar that only works if nobody replies late.

## Fewer surprises

Surprises shrink when the channel, the decision, and the cadence are the same ones you started with.

Show work earlier than feels comfortable. A rough page in the browser is a better surprise-killer than a polished presentation of the wrong direction. Hanabi will design in Figma when the structure is still a choice, and in the browser when type, content, and motion are the question. Either way, the founder should see the thing before it is “done.”

Flag risk when you see it, even if the fix is not ready. “The product photos are different crops, and the grid will look unfinished unless we recrop” is a useful note on Tuesday. The same note on the day of launch is a surprise.

Keep the tone plain. You do not need cheerleading, and you do not need a crisis voice for an ordinary delay. Say what is true, what you recommend, and what you need. That is the communication a build can run on.

Those habits are one of five behaviors worth judging a studio by. The wider set is in [quality, clean code, flexibility, speed, and communication](/blog/the-hanabi-difference-in-practice).
